Overview

The objective of this notebook is to document our validation strategy for applying stochastic character mapping (SCM) as a technique for reconstructing somatic genotype evolution given a phylogenetic tree, substitution model, and a data set of observed genotype states at the tips (see Bollback 2006 and Revell 2024). As a ground-truth somatic phylogeny data set does not yet exist, we will leverage simulation as a framework for validation.

This notebook will first describe the approach, key functions, and expected outcomes. Afterwards, additional layers of technical and biological variation will be introduced, including:

  • Sample size

  • Sequencing depth

  • Missing data

  • Collapsing branch lengths equal to 0

  • Infinite sites model (ISM) violation rate

Simulating hematopoiesis

We use the publicly available rsimpop package developed by Nick Williams at the Sanger Institute to simulate hematopoiesis under a birth-death model. This package implements the Gillespie algorithm (see here for basic overview) to simulate cellular compartments under a distribution of user-defined parameters and is described in the supplementary information of Mitchell et al. 2022.

Here, we use rsimpop with parameters set following empirical estimates from the literature. Fitness coefficients manifest as bias toward symmetric division, and polygenic effects are assumed to be additive.

The libraries and functions used in this notebook are tracked in simphy_functions.R.

Distribution of fitness effects (DFE)

rsimpop encodes fitness as increased rates of symmetric division (i.e., birth) for clones bearing a driver mutation. Here, we draw fitness effects from a gamma distribution using the parameters described in Extended Data Fig 12 of Mitchell et al. 2022.

SEED <- 1212121

# DFE function
fitnessFn <- genGammaFitness(shape = 0.47, 
                             rate = 34, 
                             seed = SEED) 

# Plot DFE
hist(sapply(1:1e4, function(x) exp(fitnessFn()) - 1),
     breaks = 100, xlim = c(0, 0.5),
     xlab = "Selection coefficient", main = "")

Simulate HSC population

Using the DFE above, we can simulate hematopoiesis with stochastic introduction of driver mutations using the run_driver_process_sim() wrapper in rsimpop. This function has several important parameters which will be defined below:

  • simpop = NULL: Default setting; do not use a pre-existing simpop object

  • initial_division_rate = 0.1: Default setting; parameter estimate for HSCs during development; only effects early population growth phase.

  • final_division_rate = 1/365: Default setting; parameter estimate for HSCs during adulthood (concordant with the estimates in Mitchell et al. 2022).

  • target_pop_size = 1e5: Default setting; mean parameter estimate for HSC population size at adulthood (concordant with the ABC estimates in Mitchell et al. 2022).

  • nyears = 50: User-defined age at collecting data. Validation will integrate across a distribution of ages.

  • fitness = fitnessFn: User-defined fitness function defined above

  • drivers_per_cell_per_day = 2.0e-3 / 365: User-defined count of driver mutations entering the population per day. This is the mean value estimated by ABC in Mitchell et al. 2022.

The functions get_subsampled_tree() and get_elapsed_time_tree() sample a subset of the total cellular phylogeny and re-scale the branch lengths given a fixed somatic mutation rate (i.e., \(16.8 \: \textrm{mutations per cell per year}\) estimated in Mitchell et al. 2022). Here, we simulate a population of \(P = 10,000\) HSCs, and subsequently sample \(N = 100\) tips.

# Simulation seed
initSimPop(SEED, bForce = TRUE)

# Run rsimpop
sim <- run_driver_process_sim(
  simpop                   = NULL,  
  initial_division_rate    = 0.1,  
  final_division_rate      = 1/365,   
  target_pop_size          = 1e5, 
  nyears                   = 80,  
  fitness                  = fitnessFn, 
  drivers_per_cell_per_day = 2.0e-3 / 365  
)

# Sample 100 cells from the HSC population
st <- get_subsampled_tree(sim, 100)

# Re-scale the phylogeny by mutations
st_mut <- get_elapsed_time_tree(st, 
                                mutrateperdivision = 0, 
                                backgroundrate = 16.8/365)

# Plot driver events on the phylogeny
plot_tree_events(st_mut,
                 cex.label = 0,
                 legpos = NULL,
                 mar = c(3,3,3,5))
mtext("Mutation burden (count)", side = 4, line = 3)

From the simulated history, we need to extract the phylo object from the simpop output.

The get_phylo_object() function takes the output from rsimpop::get_elapsed_time_tree() and extracts the phylogenetic component while also propagating driver information into the $driver_info slot of the output. Below, we’ll plot the driver events drawn from the full population.

# Get tree from simulation object
tr <- get_phylo_object(st_mut)

# Plot fitness distribution
sim$cfg$drivers %>%
  mutate(pop = "Total") %>%
  bind_rows(st_mut$cfg$drivers %>%
              mutate(pop = "Sampled")) %>%
  mutate(pop = factor(pop, levels = c("Total", "Sampled"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitness, fill = pop)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.75, 
                 position = "identity",
                 bins = 20) +
  scale_fill_npg(guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~pop, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  labs(x = "Fitness coefficient",
       y = "Count")

To compare this ground-truth tree (where branch lengths are scaled by the true mutation counts) against a molecular phylogeny, we need to re-scale these mutation counts by the size of the analyzable genome. Scaling will also account for the reduced genome access, as only genomic positions passing a genome-accessibility filter are the only loci realistically analyzed during phylogenetic inference (we use the 1000 Genomes Project GRCh38 strict accessibility mask).

Note that the branch lengths produced using the methods above will be orders of magnitude smaller than the branch lengths fit by maximum-likelihood methods (e.g., CellPhy), as the latter are scaled to the number of sites in the alignment (not the whole genome). The scale_branches_to_subs_per_site() function reads a bed file and divides $edge.length by the sum of the masked region.

  Sample tree's L: 89503
Rescaled tree's L: 3.925e-05

Extracting mutation history truth

rsimpop tracks mutation origin alongside the “ground truth” simulated history; thus, we can use these mutations to reconstruct a VCF-like structure that can later be used for SCM validation.

# Extract phyletic patterns per mutation
mut_mat <- create_mut_df(tr)

# Preview mutation matrix
mut_mat %>% 
  filter(is_driver) %>%
  select(1:9) %>%
  head() %>%
  knitr::kable()
mutation_id is_driver selection_coefficient is_ism_violation n_origins edge s1 s2 s3
9eab5e106b97 TRUE 0.1561443 FALSE 1 12 0 0 0
ff5d4ba6c61c TRUE 0.0028901 FALSE 1 33 0 0 0
68428b295a3b TRUE 0.0373747 FALSE 1 33 0 0 0
146bbd275beb TRUE 0.0043295 FALSE 1 87 0 0 0
2aff399e0e13 TRUE 0.0710599 FALSE 1 93 0 0 0
57744887c3ef TRUE 0.0220982 FALSE 1 122 0 0 0

The create_mut_df() function above takes the subsampled phylo object output by get_phylo_object() to create a data frame, where records correspond to “mutations”, and fields are defined as follows (in order):

  1. mutation_id <chr>: unique hash identifier for each record
  2. is_driver <lgl>: Boolean for whether record is a driver mutation
  3. selection_coefficient <dbl>: fitness coefficient, \(s\), if is_driver == TRUE; otherwise NA
  4. is_ism_violation <lgl>: Boolean for whether a record corresponds to an ISM violation
  5. n_origins <int>: Number of true origins for record
  6. edge <chr>: Edge number (in input phylo order) for record’s origin(s).
  7. [s1, s2, ..., sN+1] <dbl>: Remaining mutation array encoded with presence/absence (1 or 0) for whether the mutation is inherited by the tip. As an outgroup (without any mutation) is always introduced by get_subsampled_tree(), the number of fields in this component of the dataframe will equal \(N + 1\).

Thus, for \(N\) sampled tips and a total tree length of \(V\) (i.e., \(V\) mutations), the resulting data frame will be \((N + 7)\times V\) (6 metadata columns plus \(N+1\) sample columns, per points 1-7 above). Note that introducing ISM violations will reduce the total matrix size, as introduce_ism_violations() merges records (see Simulating ISM violations below).

The combination of $edge and the mutation array patterns can be used to trace a mutation’s ancestry. For example:

Mutation events on edge 12 are inherited by the following tips:
 s4 to s64

The extension of this approach for ISM violations (\(\ge 2\) origins) will be discussed in Simulating ISM Violation below.

Simulating sequence-read data

The output of create_mut_df() is then passed to the simulate_DP_and_AD() function to simulate sequence-read data. Default parameters are set such that they mimic the structure of “cleaned” data described in Coorens et al. 2025and/or modeled distribution parameters in Mitchell et al. 2022.

  • G: Matrix output by create_mut_df()

  • D_bar = 20: Target mean sequencing depth across the whole matrix

  • min_cov = 6: Lower depth bound a site must clear to pass QC (Sequoia-style min_cov)

  • max_cov = 250: Upper depth bound (excludes repeat/mapping-artifact loci)

  • site_sdlog = 0.5: Log-scale spread of per-site coverage bias (GC/mappability)

  • sample_sdlog = 0.3: Log-scale spread of per-sample library depth variation

  • theta = 8: Negative-binomial dispersion for residual (post-QC) depth noise

  • rho_max = 0.1: Beta-binomial overdispersion ceiling a site must clear (Sequoia snv_rho)

  • site_conc_shape = 4: Gamma shape for the distribution of per-site VAF concentration

  • site_conc_rate = 0.3: Gamma rate for the distribution of per-site VAF concentration

  • error_rate = 0.002: Sequencing/mapping error rate (alt reads at true hom-ref sites)

  • dropout_rate = 0.00: \(P(\textrm{complete allelic dropout} | \textrm{truly heterozygous site})\)

sim_reads <- simulate_DP_and_AD(G = mut_mat,
                                seed = SEED)
glimpse(sim_reads)

The simulate_DP_and_AD() function will generate a list with the following slots:

  • $DP [stochastic]: Data frame containing simulated sequence depth at each site \(v\) per sample \(n\). Thus, \(\texttt{DP}_{nv} \sim \textrm{NB} (\mu_{nv} = \texttt{sample\_factor}_n \times \texttt{site\_factor}_v, \theta = \texttt{theta})\)

  • $AD [stochastic]: Data frame containing simulated variant allele depth at each site \(v\) per sample \(n\). For samples without mutation, \(\texttt{AD}_{nv} \sim \textrm{Binom}(n = \texttt{DP}_{nv}, p = \texttt{error\_rate})\). For samples bearing mutation, \(\texttt{AD}_{nv} \sim \textrm{Binom}(n = \texttt{DP}_{nv}, p \sim Beta(\alpha = \beta = \frac{1}{2}\texttt{site\_conc}_{nv}))\)

  • $site_factor [stochastic]: Vector containing scaling factors for each \(v\) simulated locus; \(\texttt{site\_factor}_v \sim \textrm{LogN}_{tr} (\mu = 0, \sigma = \texttt{site\_sdlog}, a = \frac{\texttt{min\_cov}}{\texttt{D\_bar}}, b = \frac{\texttt{max\_cov}}{\texttt{D\_bar}})\)

  • $sample_factor [stochastic]: Vector containing scaling factors for each \(n + 1\) sampled tips (\(+1\) for the added outgroup); \(\texttt{sample\_factor}_n \sim \textrm{LogN}_{tr} (\mu = 0, \sigma = \sigma_v, a = \frac{\texttt{min\_cov}}{\texttt{D\_bar}}, b = \infty)\)

  • $site_conc [stochastic]: Vector containing symmetric beta distribution shape parameters used to simulate $AD at each \(NV\) site; \(\texttt{site\_conc}_v \sim \Gamma_{tr}(\alpha = \texttt{site\_conc\_shape}, \beta = \texttt{site\_conc\_rate},a = \frac{(1 - \texttt{rho\_max})}{\texttt{rho\_max}},b = \infty)\)

  • $site_rho [deterministic]: Beta-binomial’s \(\rho\) parameter for each \(v\) site; \(\rho_{v} = \frac{1}{(1 + \texttt{site\_conc}_v)}\)

  • $dropout [stochastic]: Boolean vector for whether a sample \(n\) experiences allelic dropout at site \(v\).

Below, we’ll visualize the realized distribution of mean read depth across all sites and samples under the function’s default parameters.

From the simulate_DP_and_AD() output (<list>), the $AD and $DP slots are used to compute Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods following the fixed-error-rate GATK model (DePristo et al. 2011).

sim_genotypes <- simulate_GQ_PL_GT(AD = sim_reads$AD,
                                   DP = sim_reads$DP)
glimpse(sim_genotypes)

Finally, we will sample sites from the human genome and assign these to the records held in sim_genotypes. These sites will then be threaded into a function to create a VCF-like data frame. Later, this VCF-like data structure will be exported as a VCF file that can be used as input for SCM.

mut_table <- sample_mutation_loci(nrow(sim_genotypes$GT),
                                  seed = SEED)
vcf_df <- build_vcf_df(G = mut_mat,
                       DP = sim_reads$DP,
                       AD = sim_reads$AD,
                       gl = sim_genotypes,
                       edges = mut_mat$edge,
                       mut_table = mut_table)

The VCF-like data frame can be exported as a VCF file with write_vcf_df(); we will write the ground-truth molecular phylogeny to file alongside it.

                                      pattern = "AC=0")),
             file = "test_sim/test_sim.vcf",
             tree = tr)
write.tree(tr_mol, file = "test_sim/test_sim.nwk")

Testing the SCM framework on simulated data

Given the simulated tree and somatic variants above, SCM can be performed to infer the evolutionary history of somatic variants given simulated read data. Here, we’ll use the ground truth tree and just test the performance of SCM in reproducing each variant’s origin on the tree. In practice, SCM would be performed on a molecular phylogeny inferred from the VCF file above.

The three critical components for modeling somatic SNVs with SCM are (1) the phylogeny with branch lengths measured in substitutions per site, (2) the VCF file with somatic SNVs and their associated confidence metrics (PL scores), and (3) a genotype substitution model fit to the phylogeny. Below, we’ll use a substitution model fit with CellPhy to the ground truth tree and the observed data.

The CellPhy command for fitting unphased genotype substitution model (\(Q_{GT10}\)) parameters, \(\theta\) , is the following:

cellphy.sh \
    RAXML \
    --evaluate \
    --msa path/to/test_sim.vcf \
    --msa-format vcf \
    --model GT10+FO \
    --tree path/to/test_sim.nwk \
    --prefix cellphy \
    --threads 8 \
    --force perf_threads

The function above also produces a phylogeny with branch lengths recomputed according to the fit values of \(\hat{\theta}\). However, the topology of the tree remains identical:

Validating SCM output with “ground-truth” tree

The SCM Snakemake pipeline was run on the simulated data above with 100 SCM replicates per record. Below, we’ll compare the count of true mutations generated along an edge to the count of inferred mutations.

With the edge-wise summary above, we see that SCM underestimates edge lengths relative to ground truth. Underestimation may be due to either a preponderance of mutations that lack sufficient evidence to be assigned to the phylogeny at all, or mutations that are assigned to incorrect branches.

Quantifying error

We first explore mutations that are not assigned at all to the phylogeny:

These plots show strong evidence that both GQ and DP scores stratify between mutations assigned and those missing from the tree. A Mann-Whitney U test for either quantity is statistically significant (\(p=\) 1.05^{-273} and 0, respectively). This conservative quality of SCM, while limiting the total precision of the inferred history relative to ground-truth, is nonetheless valuable for accuracy.

Next, we assess concordance between the SCM-inferred origins for the mutations and compare to ground truth. To achieve this, we can measure whether each mutation shares the same bipartitions between the ground truth and inferred history. This approach leverages the function compare_scm_edges(), a wrapper for several other functions that computes the bipartitions for each sim_tree and scm_tree inputs, matches both topologies by these bipartitions, and then computes the distance between the inferred edge(s) and the ground truth edge(s).

[1] "Edge-mapping concordance: 0.998"

Here, we measure distance as a symmetric, nearest-neighbor sum between the inferred and truth edges: \[ \Delta(S,T) = \sum_{e \in S}\min_{t \in T}d(t,e) + \sum_{t \in T}\min_{e \in S}d(t,e), \]

where \(S = {e_1, \dots, e_k}\) is the set of SCM-inferred edges for a mutation and \(T = t_1, \dots, t_m\) is the set of valid edges that can be assigned for a mutation. The first term penalizes each inferred edge for its distance from the nearest true origin (misplaced or spurious assignments), and the second penalizes each true mutation for its distance from the nearest inferred edge (origins SCM failed to recover). An assignment is correct only when \(S = T\). Since we use SCM to assign mutations to edges, not nodes, \(d(\cdot,\cdot)\) is the line-graph (edge-adjacency) distance: the distance two edges would have as vertices of the tree’s line graph, where two edges are adjacent (distance 1) exactly when they share an endpoint node. Concretely, for edges \(e=(p_e,c_e)\) and \(f=(p_f,c_f)\) (parent node, child node),

\[ d(e,f) = 1 + \min\big(d_{\text{node}}(p_e,p_f),\, d_{\text{node}}(p_e,c_f),\, d_{\text{node}}(c_e,p_f),\, d_{\text{node}}(c_e,c_f)\big), \quad e \neq f, \]

with \(d(e,e)=0\) and \(d_{\text{node}}(\cdot,\cdot)\) the node-to-node edge-count distance. This makes sibling edges \(d = 1\) apart rather than \(2\), and an edge and its immediate parent edge \(d = 1\) apart as well.

To account for the tree topology in this metric (and bound the value \([0,1]\)), we normalize by the tree’s line-graph diameter \(D\) – the largest \(d(e,f)\) between any two edges of the tree – times the total number of edges compared, \(|S| + |T|\). Thus,

\[ \Delta_{norm}(S,T) = \frac{1}{(|S| + |T|) \times D}\left(\sum_{e \in S}\min_{t \in T}d(t,e) + \sum_{t \in T}\min_{e \in S}d(t,e)\right) \in [0,1]. \]

Because two distinct edges are always at least \(1\) apart, a value of \(0\) occurs exactly when the inferred and true edge sets coincide, and a value of \(1\) corresponds to an inferred history as far as two edges can possibly be from one another (given the tree’s topology).

A visual example of this metric is provided below:

Below is a histogram of these distance metrics for mutations with discordant mapping(s):

These data suggest that when a mutation is misplaced on the phylogeny, they’re misplaced relatively near by the ground-truth.

Placement error for ISM mutations

A major error-modality here appears is low depth. For example, the variant at chr10:7337951 ought to be present in s4|s5|s6|s7|s8|s9, but SCM misplaces the mutation with a distance, \(d\), of r line_graph_distance(incorrect.df %>% filter(locus == "chr10:7337951") %>% pull(true_edge) %>% as.integer(), incorrect.df %>% filter(locus == "chr10:7337951") %>% pull(assigned_edge) %>% as.integer(),``tr_mol``, node_edge_distances(tr_mol)). Upon examination, these VCF records show that low simulated depth is a likely driver of this observation:

sample GT DP AD GQ PL
s4 0/1 4 2,2 99 255,0,255
s5 0/0 4 4,0 12 0,12,255
s6 0/1 16 8,8 99 255,0,255
s7 0/1 12 4,8 99 255,0,255
s8 0/1 5 1,4 99 255,0,255
s9 0/0 8 8,0 24 0,24,255

If we visualize the true origin of the mutation (blue) and compare to the inferred origin (red), the result is consistent with the sparse evidence in the VCF.

If we aggregate across all mutations that were mismapped to a single branch (i.e., these are mutations with single origins and inferred to have a single origin, only misplaced relative to truth) and aggregate simulated sequence read information, we observe the following:

This observation motivates stringent filtering at the scale of genotype quality.

For many of the false-positives listed above, these represent nested events where an ancestral branch is assigned the transition and a descent is incorrectly inferred to possess a reversion.

Effect of branch length

As SCM simulates genotype evolution according to a continuous-time Markov chain modeled as a Poisson process, the probability that a mutation occurs along an edge and that edge’s length are exponentially related where,

\[ f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}, ~~~ \lambda = -q_{ii}. \]

In this context, \(t\) is the edge length (measured in molecular time: substitutions per site) and \(-q_{ii}\) is the diagonal element of the genotype substitution matrix \(Q\) in state \(i\). This example is pulled directly from equation 4 in Bollback et al. 2006. Because we only simulate mutations that transition unphased genotypes from homozygous to heterozygous states, we will plot the relationship between edge length and the unconditional state transition probability for [A/A, C/C, G/G, T/T] below. Note that because we randomly select mutation loci from the human genome, the frequency (\(\pi\)) of each genotype is relatively equal (this is not expected to be the case for somatic variants, where C>T are the most common).

However, when we plot the relationship between mapping accuracy and edge length, we see relatively stable performance – this will require further validation across a larger posterior distribution of simulations.

Simulating ISM violations

To avoid changing the source code of Rsimpop to introduce infinite sites model (ISM) violations at the cellular dynamics phase, ISM violations will instead be introduced post-hoc. To accommodate the differential effects of mutations on the phylogenetic history of each simulated population, ISM violations will be introduced in a fashion that matches on fitness coefficients.

Background

To start with, we’ll use the principles of the birthday paradox to estimate the expected count of ISM violations to introduce into the population. Notably, we’ll assume a fixed mutation rate across the simulated genome, but in practice, mutation rate heterogeneity is a focal research topic in this study. The simulated history above assumes a fixed somatic mutation rate across the genome (\(\mu = 16.8 \: \textrm{SNVs per cell per year}\)), and here we estimate the expected count of ISM violations, \(x\), using,

\[E[\textrm{ISM Violations}] \approx \frac{(\sum_{i}v_i)^2}{2L},\]

where \(\sum_{i}v_i\) is the total branch length of the sub-sampled phylogeny (measured in mutations) and \(2L\) is the diploid genome size (\(\approx 6.4 \: \textrm{gigabases}\)). In the phylogeny simulated above, this evaluates to an expected 2 ISM violations.

Introducing ISM violations

Below, we’ll use both this predicted value and/or a fixed value to introduce ISM violations into the data frame output of create_mut_df(). Note that in this implementation, we randomly draw from the mutations and match on fitness coefficient when merging another variant into the ISM class (see Alternative ISM-violation strategy below for a more reliable simulation mechanism to introduce ISM violations.

A plot is generated reflecting an example for the ISM violations introduced on the phylogeny.

# Create a `violation_spec` df to specify ism violations for introduction
viols <- data.frame(n_origins = 2,
                    count = estimate_ism_violations(tr))

# Broadcase violations onto mut_mat
mut_mat.viol <- introduce_ism_violations(mut_df = mut_mat,
                                         violation_spec = viols,
                                         seed = SEED)

# Pull example for plotting
example_viol <- mut_mat.viol %>%
  filter(is_ism_violation) %>%
  head(n = 1) %>%
  pull(edge) %>% 
  str_split(pattern = ",") %>%
  unlist() %>%
  as.integer()

# Plot example violation origins
plot.phylo(tr, direction = "downwards", cex = 0.5)
edgelabels(edge = example_viol,
           frame = "circle",
           bg = "yellow",
           text = rep("", 2),
           cex = 0.5)

From here, the whole pipeline can be repeated to generate a ground truth dataset with ISM violations for SCM:

# Simulate reads from mut_mat.viol
sim_reads.viol <- simulate_DP_and_AD(G = mut_mat.viol,
                                     seed = SEED)

# Approximate uncertainty for sim_reads
sim_genotypes.viol <- simulate_GQ_PL_GT(AD = sim_reads.viol$AD,
                                        DP = sim_reads.viol$DP)

# Simulate mutation loci
mut_table.viol <- sample_mutation_loci(nrow(sim_genotypes.viol$GT),
                                       seed = SEED)

# Build VCF structure
vcf_df.viol <- build_vcf_df(G = mut_mat.viol,
                            DP = sim_reads.viol$DP,
                            AD = sim_reads.viol$AD,
                            gl = sim_genotypes.viol,
                            edges = mut_mat.viol$edge,
                            mut_table = mut_table.viol)

# Write VCF structure to file
write_vcf_df(vcf_df.viol %>% filter(!grepl(x = INFO,
                                      pattern = "AC=0")),
             file = "test_sim/test_sim.viol.vcf",
             tree = tr)

# Write tree to file
write.tree(tr_mol, file = "test_sim/test_sim.viol.nwk")

Testing ISM violation comparisons

As a basic proof of concept before scaling up this validation pipeline, we’ll investigate whether ISM violations are accurately reconstructed on the phylogeny.

[1] "Edge-mapping concordance (with ISM-violation): 0.997"

For the mutations pre-determined to be ISM violations, we recover both as placed in the correct position.

viol_loc <- vcf_df.viol %>%
  filter(grepl(x = INFO, pattern = "ISM_VIOL=1")) %>%
  select(CHROM,POS) %>%
  mutate(loc = paste(CHROM,POS,sep="_")) %>%
  pull(loc)

edge_comp.viol.df %>% filter(locus %in% viol_loc)

Alternative ISM-violation strategy

Instead of simulating under the same gamma-DFE, we could instead sample a few random deviates from the distribution and then uniformly sample that posterior distribution. Another alternative is to encode two classes of beneficial mutation: weakly beneficial and beneficial. Either way, this

Below, we’ll simulate using a discretized gamma DFE, drawing \(K = 10\) random deviates from the distribution and uniformly sampling those during the population simulation:

# Set seed
SEED <- 1212121

# DFE function
set.seed(SEED)
fitness_sample <- rgamma(n = 10,
                         shape = 0.47, 
                         rate = 34)
sub_fitnessFn <- function() sample(fitness_sample, size = 1)


# Simulation seed
initSimPop(SEED, bForce = TRUE)
NULL
# Run rsimpop
sim_ism <- run_driver_process_sim(
  simpop                   = NULL,  
  initial_division_rate    = 0.1,  
  final_division_rate      = 1/365,   
  target_pop_size          = 1e5, 
  nyears                   = 80,  
  fitness                  = sub_fitnessFn, 
  drivers_per_cell_per_day = 2.0e-3 / 365  
)

# Sample 100 cells from the HSC population
st_ism <- get_subsampled_tree(sim_ism, 100)

Simulating a posterior distribution

We will expand the logic above to simulate a posterior distribution of histories and test for concordance between the simulated “ground-truth” and SCM. For the first pass, we will simulate relatively clean read data with simulate_DP_and_AD(). This will still yield sample-wise and site-wise variation, but minimize the effects of sequencing noise.

The parameters used for simulate_DP_and_AD() are the following:

  • D_bar = 30: Target mean sequencing depth

  • min_cov = 10: Lower depth bound

  • max_cov = 250: Upper depth bound

  • site_sdlog = 0.1: Log-scale spread of per-site coverage bias

  • sample_sdlog = 0.1: Log-scale spread of per-sample depth variance

  • theta = 8: Negative-binomial dispersion for residual depth noise

  • rho_max = 0.1: Beta-binomial overdispersion ceiling a site must clear (Sequoia snv_rho)

  • site_conc_shape = 4: Gamma shape for the distribution of per-site VAF concentration

  • site_conc_rate = 0.3: Gamma rate for the distribution of per-site VAF concentration

  • error_rate = 0.000: Sequencing/mapping error rate

  • dropout_rate = 0.00 : Allelic dropout rate

We will test performance on phylogenies where the population is \(P = 10,000\), sample size \(N = \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\), age is \(t = \{20, 40, 60, 80\}\), and the number of ISM violations is a multiple of \(X = \{1,10,100\} \times E[\textrm{ISM violations}]\), restricting to 2 origins each. For each of these parameter combinations, we’ll simulate 100 replicates (totaling \(4,800\) simulations) for \(n_{SCM} = 1,000\) replicates. Each simulation will generate the following:

  1. Sampled phylogeny for ground truth (output from scale_branches_to_subs_per_site())
  2. VCF used for simulation (output from build_vcf_df())
  3. Fit substitution matrix (fit using CellPhy)
  4. SCM H5 (output from SCM pipeline)
  5. SCM-scaled phylogeny (output from SCM pipeline)
  6. Summary of mapping concordance (output from compare_scm_edges())

As above, phylogeny will remain fixed for these simulations.
